title: Types
text:
Inference
phibble infers a column’s type from its PHP values the way R’s c() combines values:

Bools and ints combine to int, and ints and floats combine to float.
Any string makes the column a string column, and the other values are converted to text.
DateTimeInterface values make a datetime column.
Arrays and other objects make a list-column.
A column that is entirely NA is bool, R’s logical type.

$df = DataFrame::fromColumns([
    'logical' => [true, false, null],
    'whole' => [1, 2, null],
    'mixed' => [1, 2.5, null],
    'with_bool' => [true, 2, 3],
    'text' => ['a', 1, null],
    'when' => [new DateTimeImmutable('2024-03-01 09:30'), null, null],
    'nested' => [[1, 2], [3], null],
    'empty' => [null, null, null],
]);

echo $df->glimpse();
Rows: 3
Columns: 8
$ logical   <lgl> TRUE, FALSE, NA
$ whole     <int> 1, 2, NA
$ mixed     <dbl> 1.0, 2.5, NA
$ with_bool <int> 1, 2, 3
$ text      <chr> "a", "1", NA
$ when      <dttm> 2024-03-01 09:30:00, NA, NA
$ nested    <list> <1, 2>, 3, <NULL>
$ empty     <lgl> NA, NA, NA
Text read from CSV files and databases is guessed differently. The input and output guide describes that.

title: Types
Types
text:
Factors
A factor column stores an ordered list of level labels and one code per row. asFactor() sorts the unique values to make the levels unless levels are given. Numbers sort numerically and text sorts in byte order. Values that are not among explicit levels become NA.
levels() returns the labels. storage('x')->codes() returns the codes, which are 0-based indexes into the levels. An ordered factor sorts by level position.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv')->asFactor('species');

echo json_encode($penguins->levels('species')), "\n";
echo json_encode(array_slice($penguins->storage('species')->codes(), 150, 5)), "\n";

$sizes = tibble(size: ['small', 'large', 'medium', 'small'])
    ->asOrdered('size', ['small', 'medium', 'large']);

echo $sizes->arrange(['size']), "\n";
var_dump($sizes->isOrdered('size'));
["Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"]
[0,0,2,2,2]
# A tibble: 4 × 1
  size  
  <ord> 
1 small 
2 small 
3 medium
4 large 
bool(true)
The forcats functions are fct* methods. Each returns a new frame with the column’s levels changed.







Method
Effect




fctRelevel($col, $levels, after: 0)
Moves the given levels to the front, or after a position.


fctLevels($col, $levels)
Sets the full level order.


fctRev($col)
Reverses the level order.


fctInorder($col)
Orders levels by first appearance.


fctInfreq($col)
Orders levels by frequency, most common first.


fctReorder($col, $by, $summary)
Orders levels by a summary of another column, the median by default.


fctRecode($col, ['new' => 'old'])
Renames levels.


fctCollapse($col, ['new' => ['a', 'b']])
Merges levels.


fctDrop($col)
Removes levels that no row uses.



$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv')->asFactor('species');

$show = fn (string $label, DataFrame $f) => print(\str_pad($label, 26).json_encode($f->levels('species'))."\n");

$show('sorted (default)', $penguins);
$show('fctRelevel Gentoo', $penguins->fctRelevel('species', ['Gentoo']));
$show('fctInfreq', $penguins->fctInfreq('species'));
$show('fctReorder by body_mass', $penguins->fctReorder('species', 'body_mass', fn ($xs) => array_sum(array_filter($xs)) / count(array_filter($xs))));
$show('fctRev', $penguins->fctRev('species'));
$show('fctRecode', $penguins->fctRecode('species', ['Chinstrap penguin' => 'Chinstrap']));
$show('fctCollapse', $penguins->fctCollapse('species', ['brush-tailed' => ['Adelie', 'Gentoo']]));
sorted (default)          ["Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"]
fctRelevel Gentoo         ["Gentoo","Adelie","Chinstrap"]
fctInfreq                 ["Adelie","Gentoo","Chinstrap"]
fctReorder by body_mass   ["Adelie","Chinstrap","Gentoo"]
fctRev                    ["Gentoo","Chinstrap","Adelie"]
fctRecode                 ["Adelie","Chinstrap penguin","Gentoo"]
fctCollapse               ["brush-tailed","Chinstrap"]

title: Types
text:
Dates and datetimes
A date column holds DateTimeImmutable values at midnight UTC. A datetime column holds DateTimeImmutable values with their time and time zone. CSV text in ISO 8601 form is parsed as a date when it has no time, and as a datetime otherwise. Text without an offset is read as UTC.
$visits = DataFrame::fromCsvString(<<<'CSV'
    day,checked_in
    2024-01-02,2024-01-02T09:15:00Z
    2024-01-03,2024-01-03 14:40:00
    CSV);

echo $visits, "\n";
echo $visits->cast(['day' => 'float', 'checked_in' => 'float']);
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  day        checked_in         
  <date>     <dttm>             
1 2024-01-02 2024-01-02 09:15:00
2 2024-01-03 2024-01-03 14:40:00
# A tibble: 2 × 2
    day checked_in
  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 19724 1704186900
2 19725 1704292800

title: Types
Types
phibble for Laravel developers
text:
phibble works with Laravel without configuration. Its service provider is registered by package discovery, and it adds two kinds of macro:
Laravel is not a dependency. The examples on this page use Eloquent with an in-memory SQLite database that holds the penguins data, through a model with a measured() scope that keeps rows with a body mass.

title: phibble for Laravel developers
section: From a collection or query to a DataFrame
text:
From a collection or query to a DataFrame
toDataFrame() builds a frame from the rows of a collection or a query. Column types are inferred from the values, as for DataFrame::fromRows().
$df = Penguin::query()
    ->where('year', 2009)
    ->get()
    ->toDataFrame();

echo $df->select(['species', 'island', 'body_mass'])->head(3);
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species island body_mass
  <chr>   <chr>      <int>
1 Adelie  Biscoe      3725
2 Adelie  Biscoe      4725
3 Adelie  Biscoe      3075
A collection of models becomes rows of their attributes. Eloquent casts and accessors apply only when the models are loaded first, as in the example above; Penguin::query()->toDataFrame() reads the rows directly.

title: phibble for Laravel developers
section: Queries that stay in the database
text:
Queries that stay in the database
phibble() turns a builder into a lazy table. The builder’s SQL, bindings, and scopes become the table’s source, and phibble’s verbs add to that query. Nothing runs until the rows are needed, for example with collect(), printing, or nrow().
$summary = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->where('year', '>=', 2008)
    ->phibble()
    ->groupBy(['species', 'sex'])
    ->summarise([
        'n' => n(),
        'mass' => mean(col('body_mass')),
    ]);

echo $summary->collect();
# A tibble: 7 × 4
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   sex        n  mass
  <chr>     <chr>  <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie    female    51 3360.
2 Adelie    male      51 4046.
3 Chinstrap female    21 3501.
4 Chinstrap male      21 4013.
5 Gentoo    female    42 4703.
6 Gentoo    male      44 5459.
7 Gentoo    <NA>       3 4750
Global scopes such as SoftDeletes apply, because phibble reads the query through Eloquent’s toBase(). Attribute casts and accessors do not apply, because the rows come from SQL.
showQuery() returns the SQL that collect() would run. In this example a grouped filter keeps the heaviest penguin on each island. The comparison with the group maximum compiles to a window function:
$heaviest = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->phibble()
    ->groupBy(['island'])
    ->filter(col('body_mass')->eq(max(col('body_mass'))))
    ->select(['island', 'species', 'body_mass']);

echo $heaviest->showQuery(), "\n\n";
echo $heaviest->arrange(['island'])->collect();
SELECT "island", "species", "body_mass" FROM (SELECT "island", "species", "body_mass", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT "id", "species", "island", "bill_len", "bill_dep", "flipper_len", "body_mass", "sex", "year", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT *, ("body_mass" = (CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY "island") > COUNT("body_mass") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") THEN NULL ELSE (CASE WHEN COUNT("body_mass") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") = 0 THEN -9e999 ELSE MAX("body_mass") OVER (PARTITION BY "island") END) END)) AS "__phibble_keep" FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS "__phibble_row" FROM (select * from "penguins" where "body_mass" is not null) AS phibble_source) AS q1) AS q2 WHERE "__phibble_keep" = TRUE) AS q3) AS q4 ORDER BY ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row"

# A tibble: 3 × 3
# Groups:   island [3]
  island    species   body_mass
  <chr>     <chr>         <int>
1 Biscoe    Gentoo         6300
2 Dream     Chinstrap      4800
3 Torgersen Adelie         4700
Expressions that SQL cannot evaluate exactly as R does, and any PHP closure, make the table collect its rows and continue in memory. The result is then a DataFrame, and the values are the same as if the whole pipeline had run in memory. The SQL tables page lists these cases.

title: phibble for Laravel developers
text:
With phplyr
phplyr provides dplyr’s verbs as a method chain on any PHP version and as functions for PHP 8.5’s pipe operator. Its verbs call the same table methods, so a phplyr pipeline on phibble() also runs in the database:

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


use function Phplyr\{phplyr, desc, n, mean};

$summary = phplyr(Penguin::query()->phibble())
    ->filter(col('year')->ge(2008))
    ->group_by('species', 'sex')
    ->summarise(n: n(), mass: mean(col('body_mass'), na_rm: true))
    ->arrange(desc('mass'))
    ->get();


use function Phplyr\{filter, group_by, summarise, arrange, desc, n, mean};

$summary = Penguin::query()->phibble()
    |> filter(col('year')->ge(2008))
    |> group_by('species', 'sex')
    |> summarise(n: n(), mass: mean(col('body_mass'), na_rm: true))
    |> arrange(desc('mass'));

title: phibble for Laravel developers
text:
Charts with phiz
phiz is a grammar of graphics in the style of ggplot2 that produces Vega-Lite specifications. Plot::of() accepts a phibble DataFrame directly. A query can select the needed columns in the database, collect them, and plot them:
use Phiz\Plot;

$penguins = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->phibble()
    ->select(['species', 'flipper_len', 'body_mass'])
    ->collect();

$plot = Plot::of($penguins)
    ->aes(x: 'flipper_len', y: 'body_mass', color: 'species')
    ->point(alpha: 0.5)
    ->smooth(method: 'lm')
    ->labs(title: 'Body mass by flipper length', x: 'Flipper length (mm)', y: 'Body mass (g)');





For a summary, the grouping and aggregation can also run in the database, so only the summary rows reach PHP:
use Phiz\Plot;

// The grouping and the means run in the database.
$byYear = Penguin::query()
    ->measured()
    ->phibble()
    ->groupBy(['species', 'year'])
    ->summarise(['mass' => mean(col('body_mass'))])
    ->collect();

echo $byYear->head(3), "\n";

$plot = Plot::of($byYear)
    ->aes(x: 'year:O', y: 'mass', color: 'species')
    ->line()
    ->point()
    ->labs(title: 'Mean body mass by year', x: 'Year', y: 'Mean body mass (g)');
# A tibble: 3 × 3
# Groups:   species [1]
  species  year  mass
  <chr>   <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie   2007 3696.
2 Adelie   2008 3742 
3 Adelie   2009 3665.





In a Laravel view, phiz’s Blade component renders a plot, and @phizScripts loads the Vega libraries once per page:
<x-phiz :plot="$plot" />

@phizScripts
phiz also has helpers that plot phit model results, such as coefplot($fit) and effect_plot($fit, $data, 'x', by: 'g'). Its documentation covers them.

title: phibble for Laravel developers
text:
Using the result
A collected frame can be returned from a controller or passed to a view:

$df->toRows() gives a list of associative arrays, for JSON responses and Blade loops.
$df->toJson() gives the same rows as a JSON string, or the columns with toJson('columns').
$df->toCollection() returns a Laravel collection of rows.
$df->toModelData() gives the columns in the form phit’s model functions accept.

title: phibble
text:
phibble is a port of R’s tibble to PHP, with the readr-style input and output a data frame needs. A DataFrame holds typed columns, treats null as NA, and never changes in place: every operation returns a new frame.
phibble is the shared table type of a small family of packages for statistics in PHP. The other packages read and return phibble tables:
The packages talk to each other through the Table contract. DataFrame is the in-memory implementation. SqlTable implements the same contract over a SQL query, so the verbs compile to SQL and run in the database.

title: phibble
text:
Install
phibble needs PHP 8.3 or later. PHP 8.5 adds the |> pipe operator, which phibble and phplyr pipelines can use.
composer require phpstats/phibble
phibble has no required dependencies beyond PHP’s PDO extension. It works with Laravel and Doctrine query builders without depending on either.

title: phibble
text:
Where to go next

Getting started covers building frames, printing, and the verbs.
Coming from tibble maps tibble, readr, and forcats functions to phibble and lists the places where phibble differs.
Types explains type inference, casts, factors, dates, and list-columns.
Reading and writing data covers CSV, JSON, databases, and Laravel collections.
Expressions documents Phibble\Expr, the inspectable expressions that every backend evaluates the same way.
SQL tables documents SqlTable, which runs verbs in SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL.
The Table contract is for authors of new backends.

title: Expressions
text:
Phibble\Expr describes a computation over columns as a tree of objects. The in-memory DataFrame evaluates the tree, SqlTable compiles it to SQL, and phpolars maps it to Polars expressions. An expression gives the same result on each backend because every backend implements the same list of functions with R’s semantics.
A PHP closure can only be run. An expression can also be inspected, translated, and serialized. phibble’s verbs accept either, and a backend that cannot run a closure itself loads the rows and runs it in memory.

title: Expressions
Expressions
text:
Using expressions with verbs
Each verb evaluates expressions per group:

filter() keeps rows where the expression is true. NA counts as false.
mutate() adds a column with one value per row. An aggregate such as mean() gives one value per group, which is repeated for each row of the group.
summarise() needs one value per group. Anything else throws a LengthException.
arrange() sorts by expressions over the whole table, ignoring groups. Wrap a key in desc() to sort it in descending order.

$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv');

$out = $penguins
    ->filter(is_na(col('body_mass'))->not())
    ->groupBy(['species'])
    ->mutate([
        'z' => col('body_mass')->sub(mean(col('body_mass')))->div(sd(col('body_mass'))),
        'rank' => min_rank(desc(col('body_mass'))),
        'size' => case_when(
            col('body_mass')->ge(5000), 'large',
            col('body_mass')->ge(3500), 'medium',
            default: 'small',
        ),
    ])
    ->filter(col('rank')->le(2))
    ->select(['species', 'body_mass', 'z', 'rank', 'size']);

echo $out;
# A tibble: 6 × 5
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   body_mass     z  rank size  
  <chr>         <int> <dbl> <int> <chr> 
1 Adelie         4725  2.23     2 medium
2 Adelie         4775  2.34     1 medium
3 Gentoo         6300  2.43     1 large 
4 Gentoo         6050  1.93     2 large 
5 Chinstrap      4550  2.13     2 medium
6 Chinstrap      4800  2.78     1 medium
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv');

echo $penguins
    ->groupBy(['island'])
    ->summarise([
        'n' => n(),
        'mass' => mean(col('body_mass')),
        'mass_rm' => mean(col('body_mass'), na_rm: true),
        'q90' => quantile(col('body_mass'), 0.9, na_rm: true),
        'species' => n_distinct(col('species')),
        'any_heavy' => any(col('body_mass')->gt(6000), na_rm: true),
    ]);
# A tibble: 3 × 7
  island        n  mass mass_rm   q90 species any_heavy
  <chr>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <int> <lgl>    
1 Biscoe      168   NA    4716.  5670       2 TRUE     
2 Dream       124 3713.   3713.  4300       2 FALSE    
3 Torgersen    52   NA    3706.  4300       1 FALSE

title: Expressions
text:
Functions
The registry in Phibble\Expr\Functions::REGISTRY lists every function an expression may call, with its arguments and options. Calling anything else throws when the expression is built.

Scalar functions
Scalar functions return one value per row.







Function
Notes




is_na(x)
True for NA and NaN.


if_else(cond, true, false, missing:)
missing is used where cond is NA.


case_when(c1, v1, c2, v2, ..., default:)
The first true condition wins. NA conditions count as false.


coalesce(x, y, ...)
The first non-NA value.


x->isIn([...])
Never NA. NA is in the set only if NA is listed.


between(x, low, high)
Inclusive. NA if any argument is NA.


na_if(x, y)
NA where x == y.


near(x, y, tol:)
Equality within a tolerance.


abs, sqrt, exp, log(x, base:), log10, floor, ceiling
Math functions.


round(x, digits:)
Rounds as R 4 does.


as_int, as_float, as_string, as_bool
Casts with R’s as.*() rules.


paste0(...), paste(..., sep:)
NA becomes the text NA, as in R.





Text functions (stringr)
As in stringr, a pattern given as text is a regular expression. phibble uses PCRE and matches by Unicode character; stringr uses ICU, and the two agree on common patterns. fixed('...') matches the text literally, and regex('...', ignore_case: true) sets options.







Function
Notes




str_detect, str_starts, str_ends (with negate:)
str_starts and str_ends anchor the pattern.


str_count(x, pattern)
Non-overlapping matches.


str_extract(x, pattern)
The first match, or NA.


str_extract_all(x, pattern), str_split(x, pattern)
A list-column. NA gives a list holding NA.


str_split_i(x, pattern, i)
The i-th piece; negative i counts from the end; NA when out of range.


str_replace, str_replace_all
\1 in the replacement refers to a group. An NA replacement gives NA where the pattern matches.


str_pad(x, width, side:, pad:)
side is left (default), right, or both.


str_trunc(x, width, side:, ellipsis:)
side is right (default), left, or center.


str_to_upper, str_to_lower, str_to_title, str_squish
Title case capitalizes after a hyphen but not after an apostrophe, as ICU does.


str_length, str_trim(x, side:), str_sub(x, start, end)
str_sub is 1-based and inclusive; negative positions count from the end.


str_lower, str_upper
Aliases of str_to_lower and str_to_upper.





Dates and times (lubridate)
Date functions accept dates and datetimes, and a date stays a date: results such as floor_date(d, 'month') or d + days(1) are dates when d is.







Function
Notes




ymd, dmy, mdy, ymd_hms, dmy_hms, mdy_hms (with tz:)
Parse text. Separators are optional; invalid input gives NA.


parse_date_time(x, orders, tz:)
Orders made of Y, y, m, d, H, M, and S, such as 'Ymd HMS'; the first that fits wins.


year, month, day, yday, quarter, hour, minute, second
Parts as numbers.


wday(x, week_start:)
1 is Sunday by default, as in lubridate; week_start: 1 makes Monday 1.


floor_date, ceiling_date, round_date (x, unit, week_start:)
Units from second to year, with multiples such as '15 minutes'. ceiling_date moves a date that is already on a boundary to the next one, as lubridate does for dates.


seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years
Periods, used as col('d')->add(months(1)). Month and year arithmetic that lands on a date that does not exist gives NA.


difftime(x, y, units:)
A number in secs, mins, hours, days (default), or weeks. date - date gives days and datetime - datetime seconds.


with_tz(x, tz), force_tz(x, tz)
The same instant in another zone; the same clock time in another zone (NA for a time the zone skips).


today(tz:), now(tz:)
Read Phibble\Expr\Clock, which tests can freeze.





Aggregates
An aggregate returns one value per group. Each takes na_rm:, which is false by default, so an aggregate over a group containing NA returns NA unless na_rm: true.







Function
Notes




n()
Rows in the group.


sum, mean, median, min, max
sum of no values is 0 and mean is NaN.


sd, var_
Sample statistics, with n - 1.


quantile(x, p), iqr(x)
R’s default type 7. These throw on NA unless na_rm: true, as R does.


n_distinct(x, ...)
Counts NA as a value unless na_rm: true. Takes several columns.


first, last, nth(x, n)
Take default: and order_by:. Negative n counts from the end.


any, all
Three-valued, as in R.





Window functions
A window function returns one value per row, computed over the rows of the group in row order.







Function
Notes




lag(x, n:, default:, order_by:), lead(...)
Shift values within the group.


row_number(x)
Ranks with ties broken by position. Without x, the row’s position.


min_rank, dense_rank, percent_rank, cume_dist
NA values stay NA and are not counted. Pass desc(x) to rank in descending order.


ntile(x, n:)
Splits rows into n groups of nearly equal size, larger groups first.


cumsum, cumprod, cummean, cummin, cummax
Every value after the first NA is NA.


cumall, cumany
Follow dplyr’s NA rules.


consecutive_id(...)
Increments when any argument changes.



$sales = tribble(
    ['store', 'week', 'units'],
    ['a', 1, 10], ['a', 2, 14], ['a', 3, 9],
    ['b', 1, 7], ['b', 2, 7], ['b', 3, 12],
);

echo $sales
    ->groupBy(['store'])
    ->mutate([
        'prev' => lag(col('units')),
        'change' => col('units')->sub(lag(col('units'))),
        'running' => cumsum(col('units')),
        'rank' => min_rank(desc(col('units'))),
        'tile' => ntile(col('units'), n: 2),
    ]);
# A tibble: 6 × 8
# Groups:   store [2]
  store  week units  prev change running  rank  tile
  <chr> <int> <int> <int>  <int>   <int> <int> <int>
1 a         1    10    NA     NA      10     2     1
2 a         2    14    10      4      24     1     2
3 a         3     9    14     -5      33     3     1
4 b         1     7    NA     NA       7     2     1
5 b         2     7     7      0      14     2     1
6 b         3    12     7      5      26     1     2

title: Expressions
text:
NA and arithmetic
Expressions follow R’s rules for missing values and arithmetic:

Arithmetic and comparisons with NA give NA.
& and | use three-valued logic. FALSE & NA is false and TRUE | NA is true.
/ and ^ always return floats. Division by zero gives Inf, -Inf, or NaN.
%% takes the sign of the divisor, so -7 %% 3 is 2.
round() takes, of the two candidates, the one closer to the stored value, and an exact tie goes to the even digit. round(2.5) is 2, and round(2.675, digits: 2) is 2.67 because 2.675 is stored as slightly less than 2.675.
Text compares and sorts in byte order.

$df = tibble(
    a: [true, false, null, null],
    b: [null, null, true, false],
    x: [2.5, 0.5, -1.5, 2.675],
    y: [1, null, 3, 4],
);

echo $df->mutate([
    'and' => col('a')->and(col('b')),
    'or' => col('a')->or(col('b')),
    'sum' => col('y')->add(1),
    'round' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x')),
    'round2' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x'), digits: 2),

title: Expressions
The Table contract
text:
Phibble\Contracts\Table is the interface that every table backend implements. phplyr’s verbs call its methods, so a pipeline runs unchanged on any backend. phibble ships two implementations: DataFrame, which holds data in PHP arrays, and SqlTable, which compiles verbs to SQL. phpolars implements it over Polars.
This page is for authors of backends. It lists the rules that every implementation follows and the semantics of each method.

title: The Table contract
text:
Rules

Immutability. Every method returns a new table and leaves the original unchanged.
Return types. Verbs are declared to return Table. A backend may return a different implementation. SqlTable returns a DataFrame when it falls back to memory for a closure. DataFrame declares static.
NA. PHP null is NA in every column type.
Grouping. groupBy() records grouping columns as metadata. filter(), mutate(), mutateGroups(), filterGroups(), summarise(), and eachGroup() work per group. The other verbs keep the grouping.
Group order. Groups are visited in sorted key order, as in dplyr: ascending, factors by level order, NA last, and strings in byte order. filter(), mutate(), and arrange() keep the input row order.
Rowwise tables. rowwise() makes every row its own group, in row order. groups() returns its id columns.
Row closures. A row closure receives (Phibble\Row $row, Table $group). $group is the row’s group, or the whole table when ungrouped.
Expressions. Wherever a verb accepts a closure, it also accepts a Phibble\Expr\Expr, evaluated per group with the semantics in the expression reference.
Errors. An unknown column name throws Phibble\Exception\ColumnNotFound.
Countable and iterable. count() equals nrow(), and iterating yields one Phibble\Row per row.

title: The Table contract
text:
Methods

Shape and data







Method
Returns




columns()
Column names in order.


types()
Column name to Phibble\Type.


nrow(), ncol()
Row and column counts.


column($name)
One column as a list. Factors return their labels.


toRows()
A list of associative arrays.


toColumns()
An array of lists by column name.


collect()
The rows as an in-memory DataFrame. A DataFrame returns itself.





Verbs







Method
Semantics




select($names)
Keeps the named columns in the given order. Grouping columns are always kept.


filter($predicate)
Keeps rows where the closure or expression is true. NA counts as false.


filterGroups($fn)
Runs $fn once per group with the group’s table. It returns one value per row, and truthy values keep the row.


mutate($columns)
Adds or replaces columns. A value is a row closure, an expression, a list with one value per row, or a scalar. Later entries see earlier ones. Replaced columns keep their position.


mutateGroups($columns)
Like mutate(), but a closure runs once per group and returns a list for the group’s rows or a scalar. This is the primitive for window functions.


rename($map)
Renames columns, with new => old entries as in dplyr.


arrange($keys)
Sorts stably. Keys are names, [name, 'asc'|'desc'] pairs, or expressions, and NA sorts last in both directions. It ignores grouping.


groupBy($names), ungroup(), groups()
Set, clear, or read the grouping columns.


groupBy($names, drop: false), dropsEmptyGroups()
dplyr’s .drop = FALSE: grouped verbs also visit empty groups. A factor key yields every level; a non-factor key yields its observed values, or NA under an empty group. Row verbs keep the flag; groupBy() and ungroup() reset it.


rowwise($idColumns), isRowwise()
Set or read rowwise mode. groupBy() and ungroup() clear it.


eachGroup()
Yields ['key' => [...], 'table' => Table] for each group, with ungrouped tables. An ungrouped table yields one group with an empty key.


summarise($aggregates)
Returns one row per group: the keys, then one column per entry. Each entry is a closure given the group’s table or an expression of size 1. The result drops the last grouping level, and a rowwise table keeps its id columns. The optional second argument is dplyr’s .groups: 'drop_last' (the default), 'drop', 'keep', or 'rowwise'.


distinct($names)
Keeps the first row of each combination of the named columns (and the grouping columns), and only those columns. An empty list means all columns.


pivotLongerSpec($spec, dropNa:)
tidyr’s pivot_longer_spec(). Spec rows are ['.name' => source, '.value' => value column, ...name parts]. Output: id columns, name parts, then one column per .value; each input row yields one row per name-part combination in spec order. Values combine by vctrs rules.


pivotWiderSpec($spec, idColumns:, valuesFill:)
tidyr’s pivot_wider_spec(). Spec rows are ['.name' => new column, '.value' => values column, ...names_from values]. New columns follow spec order; rows follow the first appearance of each id combination. Duplicates make every new column a list-column and raise tidyr’s warning.


take($indices)
Rows by 0-based position, in the given order. A null index gives an all-NA row. Keeps types, factor levels, and grouping.


slice($offset, $length), head($n)
Rows by position. These ignore grouping.


join($other, $by, $type, ...)
Joins with dplyr 1.1 semantics, described below.





Joins
join() takes the other table, a list of conditions, and the join type: inner, left, right, full, semi, anti, or cross. A cross join takes no conditions. The conditions follow dplyr’s join_by(), and all of them must hold:

'k', [$l, $r], or $l => $r: equality.
[$l, $op, $r] with $op in ==, >=, >, <=, or <: a comparison.
['closest', $l, $op, $r], at most one per join: of the y rows that satisfy the other conditions and the comparison, keep only those with the largest $r (for >= and >) or the smallest (for <= and <). Ties keep every tied row.

dplyr’s between(), within(), and overlaps() are expressed as pairs of comparisons.

Columns. The result has x’s columns, then y’s columns. Clashing names get the suffixes, .x and .y by default.
Keys. keep is null by default. Equality keys then come from x only, and for rows that only y has (right and full joins) they are filled from y’s keys. Columns used in comparisons are kept from both tables. With keep: true every key column is kept from both tables. keep: false throws when a comparison or closest condition is present, as in dplyr.
Rows. Rows follow x’s order, and each x row’s matches follow y’s order. Right and full joins then add y’s unmatched rows in y’s order. Semi and anti joins keep x’s rows and columns and never duplicate rows.
Matching. NA keys match each other unless naMatches: false. In a comparison, NA against NA satisfies >= and <= but not > or <, and NA never matches a value. 1 matches 1.0, and a factor matches text by its label.
Options. multiple picks all, any, first, or last match per x row. relationship (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many) throws when the data violates it. Without it, an unexpected many-to-many equality join raises a warning, as dplyr does. unmatched: 'error' throws when the join would drop rows.
Grouping. The result keeps x’s grouping.

title: The Table contract
text:
Errors and allowed differences
DataFrame follows R, and other backends match it. The following rules apply where R raises an error or where exact agreement is impractical.

quantile() and iqr() over values that include NA, without na_rm: true, throw an error, as R does. A backend must not return NA.
A summary entry that is not size 1 throws LengthException, and the message mentions reframe().
Aggregates over zero rows may return NA. DataFrame returns R’s values (NaN for mean(), Inf and -Inf for min() and max()). This case only arises for an ungrouped table with no rows.
as_string() on doubles with very large or very small magnitudes may differ from R’s scientific notation. Phibble\Column\Infer::formatFloat() states R’s rule: 15 significant digits, in fixed or scientific notation, whichever is shorter.

title: The Table contract
text:
Testing a backend
The simplest test of a backend is to run the same operations on the backend and on DataFrame and compare the results. tests/SqlTest.php does this for SqlTable. It loads the same data into a database, runs each operation both ways, and compares the collected rows. It also runs every case in tests/fixtures/expr/expected.json, the dplyr results that tests/r/expr.R produces, so each backend is checked against R as well as against DataFrame.

title: Backends
text:
phibble separates what a pipeline does from where it runs. Every verb is part of the Phibble\Contracts\Table interface, and three classes implement it:
Code written against Table, including phplyr’s verbs, runs on any of them. A pipeline gives the same result on each backend, because a backend that cannot run a step exactly (a PHP closure, or a function with no exact translation) hands that step to DataFrame and continues. The Table contract page states the rules each backend follows.

title: Backends
text:
Choosing and switching
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phibble\{tbl, polars};
use function Phibble\Expr\{col, mean, n};

$df = DataFrame::fromCsv('sales.csv');      // in memory
$sql = tbl($pdo, 'sales');                     // in the database
$fast = polars($df);                        // in Polars

$summary = fn ($t) => $t
    ->filter(col('units')->gt(0))
    ->groupBy(['store'])
    ->summarise(['n' => n(), 'avg' => mean(col('price'))]);

$summary($df);             // a DataFrame
$summary($sql)->collect();    // runs as one SQL query
$summary($fast)->collect();   // runs in Polars
collect() turns any table into a DataFrame. PolarsTable::fromTable() and polars() move a table into Polars; tbl() opens a database table or query.

title: Backends
text:
The Polars backend
The Polars backend needs the php_polars extension from phpolars. phibble does not require it: composer.json lists it as a suggestion, and the class is only loaded when used. Expressions, joins (including join_by comparisons and rolling joins), pivots, and the lubridate and stringr functions run natively in Polars. Steps it cannot run, such as PHP closures and str_to_title(), run in DataFrame. PolarsTable::$fallbacks counts those steps.
Two kinds of list-column stay in DataFrame. Polars stores named arrays as structs, which have every key in every row, so fromTable() throws when a list-column holds named arrays with different keys. A list-column of DataFrames cannot be stored in Polars either.
The Polars test suite runs phibble’s dplyr, tidyr, lubridate, and stringr reference cases on PolarsTable and skips when the extension is not loaded.

title: Coming from tibble
text:
Differences
phibble differs from R in these places:

Whole numbers guess as int. readr guesses 1,2,3 as double. phibble guesses int, which suits PHP. Pass types: 'd' to read a double.
Positions are 0-based. addRow(before:), addColumn(before:), take(), slice(), and row() count rows and columns from 0.
String functions use fixed patterns. str_detect(), str_starts(), str_ends(), str_replace(), and str_replace_all() match literal text. SQL backends have no portable regular expressions.
There is no time-of-day type. readr’s hms columns and the t column type stay strings.
JSON keeps null values. jsonlite drops NA fields from records. toJson() writes them as null.
Datetimes are UTC. Text without an offset is read as UTC, and text with an offset is converted to UTC, as readr does.
Strings sort in byte order. Sorting, grouping, and factor levels use the C locale, as dplyr’s arrange() does. Base R’s factor() uses the system locale, which can order mixed-case levels differently.
Packed data frame columns are not supported. An unnamed table in tibble() is spliced into columns. A named one throws.

title: Development
text:
The test suite uses Pest and runs on PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. Tests that use the |> operator are in tests/Php85, which phpunit.xml loads only on PHP 8.5:

The tests that fit models need the phit extension and are skipped without it. To run them, load the extension:
php -d extension=/path/to/libphit.dylib vendor/bin/pest

text:
Database tests
tests/SqlTest.php runs against an in-memory SQLite database. It also runs against PostgreSQL and MySQL when these environment variables hold PDO DSNs:
export PHIBBLE_TEST_PGSQL="pgsql:host=127.0.0.1;port=5432;dbname=postgres"
export PHIBBLE_TEST_PGSQL_USER=postgres
export PHIBBLE_TEST_MYSQL="mysql:host=127.0.0.1;port=3306"

PHIBBLE_TEST_PGSQL_PASSWORD and PHIBBLE_TEST_MYSQL_PASSWORD set passwords. The tests only run SELECT statements over inline data and create no tables.

title: Development
text:
Documentation
The site is a Quarto project in docs/. Every example is a PHP file in docs/examples/. bin/docs-examples runs each example with docs/data as the working directory and writes its code and output to docs/examples/_<name>.md, which the pages include. Quarto never runs PHP.
bin/render-docs refreshes the examples, renders the site, and copies the result into docs/ for GitHub Pages:
PHP=php85 bin/render-docs
bin/docs-examples name refreshes one example. Set QUARTO when the quarto command is not on the path.

title: Getting started
text:
Types and NA
Each column has one type from the Phibble\Type enum: Float, Int, Bool, String, Factor, Date, DateTime, or List. Types are inferred from the values, and PHP null is NA in every type. The types guide describes inference, casts, and factors.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Verbs
DataFrames have the dplyr verbs as methods: select(), filter(), mutate(), rename(), arrange(), groupBy(), summarise(), distinct(), slice(), head(), and join(). Each returns a new frame.
filter() and mutate() accept a row closure, which receives a Row and returns a value. arrange() takes column names, or [name, 'desc'] pairs.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv');

$heavy = $penguins
    ->select(['species', 'island', 'body_mass', 'year'])
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->body_mass !== null && $r->body_mass > 5500)
    ->mutate(['kg' => fn ($r) => $r->body_mass / 1000])
    ->arrange([['body_mass', 'desc']])
    ->head(5);

echo $heavy;
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  species island body_mass  year    kg
  <chr>   <chr>      <int> <int> <dbl>
1 Gentoo  Biscoe      6300  2007  6.3 
2 Gentoo  Biscoe      6050  2007  6.05
3 Gentoo  Biscoe      6000  2008  6   
4 Gentoo  Biscoe      6000  2009  6   
5 Gentoo  Biscoe      5950  2008  5.95
The same verbs accept expressions built with col() and the helper functions. Expressions are evaluated a whole column at a time, and they are the form that SQL and Polars backends can translate.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv');

$heavy = $penguins
    ->select(['species', 'island', 'body_mass', 'year'])
    ->filter(col('body_mass')->gt(5500))
    ->mutate(['kg' => col('body_mass')->div(1000)])
    ->arrange([desc(col('body_mass'))])
    ->head(5);

echo $heavy;
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  species island body_mass  year    kg
  <chr>   <chr>      <int> <int> <dbl>
1 Gentoo  Biscoe      6300  2007  6.3 
2 Gentoo  Biscoe      6050  2007  6.05
3 Gentoo  Biscoe      6000  2008  6   
4 Gentoo  Biscoe      6000  2009  6   
5 Gentoo  Biscoe      5950  2008  5.95

title: Getting started
text:
Groups
groupBy() records grouping columns on the frame. summarise() returns one row per group, with groups in sorted order and NA last, as dplyr does. With several grouping columns, the result keeps all but the last.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv');

$summary = $penguins
    ->filter(col('body_mass')->isNa()->not())
    ->groupBy(['species', 'sex'])
    ->summarise([
        'n' => n(),
        'mass' => mean(col('body_mass')),
        'flipper' => median(col('flipper_len')),
    ]);

echo $summary;
# A tibble: 8 × 5
# Groups:   species [3]
  species   sex        n  mass flipper
  <chr>     <chr>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Adelie    female    73 3369.    188 
2 Adelie    male      73 4043.    193 
3 Adelie    <NA>       5 3540     186 
4 Chinstrap female    34 3527.    192 
5 Chinstrap male      34 3939.    200.
6 Gentoo    female    58 4680.    212 
7 Gentoo    male      61 5485.    221 
8 Gentoo    <NA>       4 4588.    216
In a grouped frame, filter() and mutate() work within each group. An aggregate inside mutate() is computed per group and repeated for each of the group’s rows:
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv')->dropNa(['body_mass']);

$centered = $penguins
    ->groupBy(['species'])
    ->mutate(['vs_species' => col('body_mass')->sub(mean(col('body_mass')))])
    ->select(['species', 'body_mass', 'vs_species'])
    ->head(4);

echo $centered;
# A tibble: 4 × 3
# Groups:   species [1]
  species body_mass vs_species
  <chr>       <int>      <dbl>
1 Adelie       3750       49.3
2 Adelie       3800       99.3
3 Adelie       3250     -451. 
4 Adelie       3450     -251.
A row closure receives the row’s group as its second argument: fn (Row $r, DataFrame $group) => ....
By default, groups are the combinations that occur in the data. With groupBy($names, drop: false), as with dplyr’s .drop = FALSE, a factor key also yields a group for each level that has no rows. Such a group has zero rows, so n() is 0 and sum() is 0.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv')
    ->asFactor('species')
    ->filter(col('species')->ne('Chinstrap'));

echo $penguins->groupBy(['species'], drop: false)->summarise(['n' => n()]);
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species       n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie      152
2 Chinstrap     0
3 Gentoo      124

title: Reading and writing data
text:
DataFrame::fromCsv() reads delimited text the way readr’s read_csv() and read_delim() do. It takes a path (files ending in .gz are decompressed) or an open stream. DataFrame::fromCsvString() reads from a string.
readr’s options are named arguments in camelCase:








Option
Default
Meaning




types
guess
Column types, as a compact string or by name.


delimiter
','
The field separator.


na
['', 'NA']
Text that is read as NA.


colNames
true
true reads a header row, false names columns X1, X2, and so on, and a list gives the names.


select
all
Columns to keep, in this order.


skip
0
Lines to skip before the header.


nMax
all
The most rows to read.


comment
''
Lines starting with this text are skipped.


quote
'"'
The quoting character.


trimWs
true
Trim spaces around unquoted values.


skipEmptyRows
true
Skip blank lines.


guessMax
1000
Rows used to guess types.


nameRepair
'unique'
How to repair empty or duplicated names.


decimalMark, groupingMark
'.', none
Number formatting, as in readr’s locale().



$text = <<<'CSV'
    # exported 2024-06-01
    id;zip;score;visited
    1;02134;3,5;2024-05-01
    2;10001;-;2024-05-03
    3;94110;4,25;2024-05-04
    CSV;

$df = DataFrame::fromCsvString(
    $text,
    types: ['zip' => 'c'],
    delimiter: ';',
    na: ['-'],
    comment: '#',
    decimalMark: ',',
);

echo $df;
# A tibble: 3 × 4
     id zip   score visited   
  <int> <chr> <dbl> <date>    
1     1 02134  3.5  2024-05-01
2     2 10001 NA    2024-05-03
3     3 94110  4.25 2024-05-04

title: Reading and writing data
text:
Column types
types accepts readr’s compact string, with one letter per column:







Letter
Type




c
string


i
int


d
float


n
float, reading numbers with grouping marks and other characters


l
bool


f
factor


D
date


T
datetime


t
string (phibble has no time-of-day type)


?
guess


_ or -
skip the column



types also accepts an array by column name. A value is a Type, a type name such as 'factor', or a letter. The key .default sets the type of every column not named.
$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv', types: 'ffddii_i');
echo $penguins->glimpse(), "\n";

$some = DataFrame::fromCsv('penguins.csv', types: ['species' => 'factor', '.default' => '_'], select: ['species']);
echo $some->glimpse();

title: Reading and writing data
Reading and writing data
text:
Writing CSV
writeCsv($path) writes a file and toCsv() returns the text. The format follows readr’s write_csv(). Values are quoted only when needed, NA is written as NA, logicals as TRUE and FALSE, dates in ISO 8601, and datetimes in UTC with a Z. Factors are written as their labels, and list-columns throw.
$df = tribble(
    ['name', 'note', 'score', 'seen'],
    ['Ana', 'likes "quotes"', 1e5, true],
    ['Ben', 'a, b', null, false],
);

echo $df->toCsv();
name,note,score,seen
Ana,"likes ""quotes""",100000,TRUE
Ben,"a, b",NA,FALSE
The options are delimiter, na, append, colNames, quote ('needed', 'all', or 'none'), escape, and eol.

SQL tables
text: Phibble\Sql\SqlTable is a table backed by a SQL query, like dbplyr’s tbl(). It implements the same Table contract as DataFrame. Verbs called with expressions are compiled into SQL, and no query runs until the rows are needed. SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL are supported.

title: SQL tables
SQL tables
text:
What compiles to SQL
These verbs compile when their arguments are expressions or column names: select(), rename(), filter(), mutate(), arrange(), groupBy(), summarise(), distinct(), slice(), head(), and join().
The compiled SQL keeps R’s semantics:

An aggregate returns NA when its group contains NA, unless na_rm: true. SQL aggregates skip NULL, so phibble adds a check on the count of non-NULL values.
Cumulative functions return NA after the first NA.
Ranks leave NA rows unranked.
isIn() never returns NA.
/ returns a float, and division by zero gives NA.
Groups in summarise() output are sorted, with NA last.

title: SQL tables
section: When the table falls back to memory
text:
When the table falls back to memory
Some arguments have no faithful SQL translation. A SqlTable then collects the rows and runs the verb in memory, and the verb returns a DataFrame. Results match DataFrame in either case. The fallbacks are:

any PHP closure,
round(), because SQL’s ROUND does not round half to even,
as_string() and as_bool(),
paste() and paste0() with arguments other than text literals, because SQL formats numbers differently from R,
regular-expression patterns, except str_detect() in MySQL (which uses ICU, as stringr does). Patterns wrapped in fixed(), and plain patterns without regular-expression characters, are translated everywhere,
str_extract(), str_extract_all(), str_split(), str_split_i(), str_to_title(), center str_trunc(), and str_pad(side: 'both'); str_pad() and str_squish() in SQLite; str_to_upper() and str_to_lower() in SQLite, whose UPPER() and LOWER() change only ASCII letters,
parsing text to dates (ymd() and the others) on columns, floor_date(), ceiling_date(), round_date(), period arithmetic, with_tz(), and force_tz(), because the result type depends on the column type, which SQL tables do not track. Date parts (year() and the others), wday(), and difftime() are translated; a call on literals only, such as ymd('2024-01-01'), is evaluated once and passed as a value,
first(), last(), and nth() without a row order (from arrange() or order_by:), or with default: or na_rm:,
iqr() outside PostgreSQL, cumprod(), and consecutive_id(),
sd() and var() in SQLite, whose formula would lose precision,
str_trim(), because R removes all Unicode white space and SQL TRIM removes spaces,
nested aggregates such as mean(x - mean(x)), summarise() entries that are not one value per group, and slice() with negative positions,
median() and quantile() outside PostgreSQL,
quantile() without na_rm: true,
median(), quantile(), and n_distinct() inside grouped mutate() or filter(), because SQL has no window form of them,
take(), eachGroup(), rowwise(), mutateGroups() with closures, and filterGroups(),
joins with multiple, relationship, or unmatched set, joins between different connections, full joins in MySQL, and full joins with NA matching in PostgreSQL.

$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$t = tbl($pdo, 'SELECT 1 AS id, 2.5 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 2, 3.5');

// Compiles to SQL.
echo get_class($t->mutate(['y' => col('x')->mul(2)])), "\n";

// round() rounds half to even in R, which SQL ROUND does not, so the rows
// are collected and the expression runs in memory.
echo get_class($t->mutate(['y' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x'))])), "\n";

// So does any closure.
echo get_class($t->filter(fn ($r) => $r->x > 3)), "\n";

echo $t->mutate(['y' => Phibble\Expr\round(col('x'))]);
Phibble\Sql\SqlTable
Phibble\DataFrame
Phibble\DataFrame
# A tibble: 2 × 3
     id     x     y
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1   2.5     2
2     2   3.5     4
SQLite compares by storage class, and it orders all text above all numbers. A column declared without a type stores bound values as text, so col('x')->gt(0) is true for every row of such a column. Declare column types (INTEGER, REAL, TEXT) when creating SQLite tables that phibble will query.

title: SQL tables
text:
Known differences
These cases can differ from DataFrame, because the database cannot represent R’s result:

MySQL has no infinity or NaN. Results that are Inf, -Inf, or NaN in R, such as x / 0, log(0), or mean() of no values, are NA in MySQL. SQLite stores infinities but has no NaN, so NaN is NA there.
Integer arithmetic beyond 64 bits fails in the database, where DataFrame switches to a double.
Joins do not warn about unexpected many-to-many matches.
Column names starting with __phibble_ are reserved for the hidden columns that keep row order and window results.

Text compares in byte order and case-sensitively, as R does: phibble applies COLLATE "C" in PostgreSQL and utf8mb4_0900_bin in MySQL to text columns wherever values are compared, sorted, grouped, or joined.

title: SQL tables
text:
Window functions
Grouped mutate() and filter() compile aggregates and window functions to OVER (PARTITION BY ...). Window functions such as lag() and cumsum() need a row order. SQL tables have none, so phibble numbers the rows of the source query when the table is opened and keeps that number through every step. Windows use the order_by: option where given, otherwise the order set by arrange(), and otherwise the source order. The same order decides the order of collected rows and breaks ties after arrange(), which is stable as in dplyr. The source order is the order in which the database returns the source query’s rows. For a stored table, add arrange() to make it explicit.
$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$sales = tbl($pdo, <<<'SQL'
    SELECT 'a' AS store, 1 AS week, 10 AS units
    UNION ALL SELECT 'a', 2, 14 UNION ALL SELECT 'a', 3, 9
    UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 1, 7 UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 2, NULL
    SQL);

$out = $sales
    ->groupBy(['store'])
    ->arrange(['store', 'week'])
    ->mutate([
        'running' => cumsum(col('units')),
        'of_best' => col('units')->div(max(col('units'), na_rm: true)),
    ]);

echo $out->showQuery(), "\n\n";
echo $out->collect();
SELECT "store", "week", "units", "running", "of_best" FROM (SELECT "store", "week", "units", "running", (CASE WHEN (CASE WHEN COUNT("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store") = 0 THEN -9e999 ELSE MAX("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store") END) = 0 THEN (CASE WHEN "units" > 0 THEN 9e999 WHEN "units" < 0 THEN -9e999 WHEN "units" = 0 THEN NULL END) ELSE CAST("units" AS REAL) / (CASE WHEN COUNT("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store") = 0 THEN -9e999 ELSE MAX("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store") END) END) AS "of_best", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT "store", "week", "units", (CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY "store" ORDER BY ("store" IS NULL), "store", ("week" IS NULL), "week", ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row" ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) > COUNT("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store" ORDER BY ("store" IS NULL), "store", ("week" IS NULL), "week", ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row" ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) THEN NULL ELSE SUM("units") OVER (PARTITION BY "store" ORDER BY ("store" IS NULL), "store", ("week" IS NULL), "week", ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row" ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) END) AS "running", "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS "__phibble_row" FROM (SELECT 'a' AS store, 1 AS week, 10 AS units
UNION ALL SELECT 'a', 2, 14 UNION ALL SELECT 'a', 3, 9
UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 1, 7 UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 2, NULL) AS phibble_source) AS q1) AS q2) AS q3 ORDER BY ("store" IS NULL), "store", ("week" IS NULL), "week", ("__phibble_row" IS NULL), "__phibble_row"
